title: Directing a project: practices applied and judging the process
blurb: Say which practice a board decision applies, and judge whether the board is directing by exception at the right decision points.
question: The executive tells the contractor's site team directly to re-sequence the works, bypassing the project manager. Is this an appropriate way to direct the project, and why?

teach.body: Formally: directing a project applies the practices through the board's approvals and checks (tab 14.3), and its effectiveness is judged against its purpose, objectives, tailoring and roles (14.1 to 14.7). In plain English: when the board approves something, ask which practice that product belongs to; when the board acts, ask whether it is directing at the right level or slipping into managing.

head: Practice
What the board does
Product
rows: Approves the PPD and quality approach
Validates highlight and end stage reports; approves exception reports
teach.caption: These four are the official extracts the exam uses. Approving a product applies the practice that owns it.

teach.body: The board is accountable for success, makes the key decisions and keeps overall control, but delegates day-to-day management to the project manager. Its objectives include authority to initiate, deliver and close, keeping the project viable, a connection to the business layer, and managing plans for post-project benefits. A board that manages tasks, or decides nothing, fails the test.

levels.label: Project board
levels.sub: Stage tolerances; stage exceptions; key decisions

levels.label: Project manager
levels.sub: Work package tolerances; day to day

items: Level: is the board deciding a stage or project matter, or meddling in work packages?
Decision point: is an authorization explicit, documented and based on the right products?
Exceptions: is it reacting to forecast breaches of stage tolerance, and referring project ones upward?
Practices: is it approving the right products (benefits, quality, risk approaches) and validating reports?
Tailoring: does the reporting suit the board's needs, for example a safety section or virtual reports?

teach.body: At Tarnside College, the board (executive Dr Elaine Fairbairn, the vice principal and head of estates as senior users, and the contractor's director as senior supplier) approves the benefits approach for 300 apprentices a year and the risk approach with a low appetite for safety risk. One governor wants safety reported at every meeting, so the board asks for a safety section in each highlight report. When Leah Whitfield forecasts an overspend beyond the governors' 3% limit, the board refers it to the governors.

teach.text: Classic traps: the board is not involved in managing product delivery and does not instruct team members directly; it directs through the project manager. A breach of PROJECT tolerance goes to the business layer, not the board. 'More control' is not always better control: reviewing every work package is the PM's job.

items: Tab 14.3: business case (benefits approach), quality (PPD, quality approach), risk (risk approach), progress (validate reports, approve exception reports).
Board: key decisions and overall control; day-to-day management delegated to the PM.
Stage exceptions to the board; project exceptions to the business layer; work package matters stay with the PM.
Tailor the board's reporting to its control needs.

summary: You can now name the practice applied by each board approval in directing a project. You can also judge whether a board is directing effectively: deciding at the right level, documenting its decisions, handling exceptions by tolerance and tailoring its reporting.

A.q: Tarnside College's project board is authorizing the Engineering Skills Centre project. It approves how the target of 300 apprentices a year will be measured and when benefits reviews will take place. Which practice is the board applying?
options: Progress, because it sets when reviews will be reported
Quality, because the apprentice target is a quality criterion
Plans, because the reviews are scheduled in the project plan
Business case, because it approves the benefits approach
A.why: Tab 14.3: the business case practice is applied in directing a project by approving the benefits management approach.

whyNot.0: Progress is applied by validating reports and approving exception reports, not by approving benefits reviews.
whyNot.1: Apprentice numbers are a benefit, not a quality criterion for a product.
whyNot.2: Benefits reviews are defined in the benefits management approach, not the project plan.

A.q: During Tarnside's structural works stage, board members compare the project manager's highlight reports with what they see on a site visit before relying on them for decisions. Which practice is the board applying?
options: Progress, because it assures fair progress reporting
Quality, because site visits check product quality
Risk, because site visits reveal new safety threats
Issues, because differences become issues to log
A.why: Tab 14.3: progress is applied in directing a project by assuring fair progress reporting through validating highlight and end stage reports.

whyNot.1: Product quality is checked through quality control; this is about the reports.
whyNot.2: New threats may be found, but the purpose here is to confirm reporting is fair.
whyNot.3: A difference might become an issue, but the board's action is validating progress reports.

A.q: When authorizing the Tarnside project, the board approves the project product description, with acceptance criteria such as 24 welding bays with fume extraction, and the approach to quality checks on the fit-out. Which practice is the board applying?
options: Plans, because the PPD is a planning product
Risk, because fume extraction is a safety control for the bays
Quality, because it approves the PPD and quality approach
Business case, because the bays deliver the benefits
A.why: Tab 14.3: quality is applied in directing a project by approving the project product description and the quality management approach.

whyNot.0: The PPD is developed through plans in starting up, but approving it with the quality approach is listed under quality.
whyNot.1: Safety is relevant, but the board's action is approving quality products.
whyNot.3: The bays lead to benefits, but approving acceptance criteria and quality checks is quality.

B.q: Tarnside's board approves the risk management approach for the Engineering Skills Centre. The approach sets probability and impact scales and reflects the college's low appetite for safety risks near the student entrance. Which practice is the board applying?
options: Quality, because it protects the students who use the site
Risk, because it approves the risk management approach
Progress, because the scales set the risk tolerance
Issues, because safety incidents are recorded as issues
B.why: Tab 14.3: risk is applied in directing a project by approving the risk management approach.

whyNot.0: Protecting students matters, but approving how risk is managed is the risk practice.
whyNot.2: Tolerances are part of progress control, but this is approval of the risk approach.
whyNot.3: Incidents that happen are issues, but the board is approving how risks are managed.

B.q: Tarnside's governors have set a project cost tolerance of 3% above the approved budget. The project manager forecasts that total cost will exceed it because of asbestos removal. Who should decide what happens next?
options: The project manager
The project board
The business layer
The senior supplier
B.why: The board decides on stage tolerance breaches; a forecast breach of project tolerance is decided by the business layer, here the governors (11.2.1, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: The PM escalates; he or she cannot decide on a breach of project tolerance.
whyNot.1: The board decides stage-level exceptions and refers project-level ones to the business layer.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier commits supplier resources; it does not decide on project tolerance breaches.

B.q: Tarnside's project manager raises an exception report forecasting that the structural works stage will exceed its time tolerance. The board considers the options and asks her to prepare an exception plan. Which directing activity is this, and which practice does responding to the exception report apply?
options: Give ongoing direction, applying progress
Authorize a stage or exception plan, applying plans
Authorize the project, applying risk
Authorize project closure, applying progress
B.why: Responding to exception reports, including requesting an exception plan, is part of give ongoing direction (14.4.3); approving exception reports applies progress (tab 14.3).

whyNot.1: The exception plan is approved later in authorize a stage or exception plan; here the board is requesting it.
whyNot.2: Authorize the project happens at the end of initiation.
whyNot.3: Closure is not being considered; the board wants an exception plan.

C.q: Tarnside's executive, Dr Elaine Fairbairn, visits the site before a governors' tour and tells the contractor's site team directly to re-sequence the works so the mezzanine looks finished. She does not involve the project manager. Is this an appropriate way to direct the project, and why?
options: Yes, because the executive is accountable for the project's success
Yes, because individual board members can give ongoing direction
No, because the contractor should be directed by the senior supplier
No, because the board delegates day-to-day direction to the PM
C.why: Directing a project delegates day-to-day management to the project manager; the board is not involved in managing product delivery, and teams take instructions from the PM (14.1, 14.3).

whyNot.0: The executive is accountable, but that does not justify bypassing the PM to manage the site.
whyNot.1: Ongoing direction can come from individuals, but it is given to the PM, not to the site team.
whyNot.2: The senior supplier commits resources, but day-to-day direction of teams comes through the PM.

C.q: A Tarnside governor wants safety reported to the board at every meeting, because the site is next to the student entrance. The board agrees that each highlight report will include a short safety section. Is this an appropriate way for the board to direct the project, and why?
options: Yes, because the project board sets the stage tolerances
Yes, because reporting can be tailored to the board's needs
No, because highlight reports are limited to reporting stage status
No, because safety concerns should go in an exception report
C.why: The content and frequency of reports can be tailored to the control the board needs; a safety section suits this site's risks (2.7, 11.2.4).

whyNot.0: The board does set stage tolerances, but that does not explain the reporting change.
whyNot.2: Highlight report content can be tailored to what the board needs.
whyNot.3: Exception reports are for forecast tolerance breaches, not routine safety reporting.

C.q: Tarnside's board decides to meet every month to read each contractor checkpoint report and approve every work package before work starts, because the estates team is inexperienced. Is this an appropriate way to direct the project, and why?
options: Yes, because an inexperienced team needs more frequent control
Yes, because the board must assure that progress reporting is fair
No, because work packages are controlled by the PM within tolerance
No, because checkpoint reports are reviewed by project assurance
C.why: The board manages by exception through stage tolerances and highlight reports; authorizing work packages and reading checkpoint reports belong to the PM in controlling a stage (14.3, 11.2.1).

whyNot.0: More frequent reporting may suit an inexperienced team, but at the PM's level, not by the board taking over work packages.
whyNot.1: The board validates highlight and end stage reports; that does not mean reviewing every checkpoint.
whyNot.3: Checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager.

reteach.title: Approve the products, steer the PM
reteach.question: Can you spot the practice behind a board approval and tell good directing from meddling?

blocks.body: Practice test: what product is the board approving or checking? Benefits approach means business case; PPD and quality approach mean quality; risk approach means risk; highlight, end stage and exception reports mean progress. Level test: is the board deciding a stage or project matter through the PM, or doing the PM's job?

head: The board...
Practice
rows: Approves the PPD and quality approach

blocks.text: A board that reads every checkpoint report or instructs team members directly is managing, not directing.

explain.body: When authorizing the project, the board approves the benefits management approach (business case practice) and the risk management approach (risk practice). Both shape how the board later judges viability and exposure.

test.q: Tarnside's board approves the document that sets out the risk procedure, the probability and impact scales and who is responsible for risk management. Which practice does this approval apply?
options: Risk
Quality
Progress
Issues
test.why: Tab 14.3: approving the risk management approach applies the risk practice.

whyNot.1: Quality is applied by approving the PPD and quality management approach.
whyNot.2: Progress is applied by validating reports and approving exception reports.
whyNot.3: The issue management approach is a different product.

explain.body: The board applies quality by approving the PPD and the quality management approach. It applies progress by validating highlight and end stage reports, so reporting is fair, and by approving exception reports.

test.q: Tarnside's board receives an exception report with options for recovering the fit-out stage, and approves it with the project manager's recommendation. Which practice is applied by approving the exception report?
options: Risk
Plans
Quality
Progress
test.why: Tab 14.3: progress is applied in directing a project by validating highlight and end stage reports and approving exception reports.

whyNot.0: Risk is applied by approving the risk management approach.
whyNot.1: The exception plan that may follow is a plan, but approving the report is progress.
whyNot.2: Quality is applied by approving the PPD and quality management approach.

explain.body: Work package matters stay with the PM. Forecast breaches of stage tolerance go to the board. Forecast breaches of project tolerance go to the business layer. Day-to-day instructions go through the PM.

test.q: A Tarnside team manager forecasts that one work package will exceed its time tolerance by two days, but the stage remains within its tolerance. Who should deal with this?
options: The project board
The project manager
The business layer
Project assurance
test.why: Work package exceptions are handled by the project manager in controlling a stage; only stage or project exceptions are escalated (14.4.3, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: The board deals with forecast breaches of stage tolerance, not work package ones.
whyNot.2: The business layer deals with project tolerance breaches.
whyNot.3: Project assurance advises the board; it does not decide on exceptions.

explain.body: An effective board makes explicit, documented decisions at stage boundaries, responds to exceptions, gives advice when asked, keeps a link to the business layer and tailors reporting to its needs. An ineffective board either micro-manages or lets decisions slide.

test.q: Tarnside's board is spread across two campuses. It agrees to receive highlight reports through an online dashboard and to hold a short video call at each stage boundary. How well does this apply directing a project?
options: Poorly, because stage decisions need the board in one room
Poorly, because highlight reports must be written documents
Well, because it tailors reporting to the board's situation
Well, because it lets the board review every work package
test.why: Tailoring the format of board reporting and meetings to the board's circumstances is good practice, as long as decisions stay explicit (2.7, 11.2.4).

whyNot.0: Decisions can be made without the board meeting in one room.
whyNot.1: Report format can be tailored, for example virtual or dashboard reporting.
whyNot.3: Reviewing every work package is not the board's role.
